title: A DC trial was nearing its end when the jury made a discovery that shocked everyone in the courtroom
description: The charges at a month-long criminal trial in Washington’s federal court last month were fairly straightforward: That one man had allegedly held up seven 7-Elevens and a few other gas stations in spri...
fullText:
The charges at a monthlong criminal trial in Washington's federal court last month were fairly straightforward: That one man had allegedly held up seven 7-Elevens and a few other gas stations in spring 2023 and stolen cars.

But the trial of Shamell Naquan Joyner had a twist. While deliberating, jurors found a Chinese yuan in one sweatshirt that was in evidence. And inside a jacket that was also part of the case, they found suspicious white powder in a folded up piece of paper. The prosecutors and judge said it appeared to be drugs.

The DC US Attorney's Office, law enforcement on the case and the defense team hadn't known.

The events of the jury deliberation raised eyebrows across the federal court in recent days, as word spread of what happened.

During deliberations, jurors are allowed to review evidence that is presented during the trial. Had the suspected drugs and yuan been part of the prosecution's case ahead of trial, it could have supported the case. But because it was a surprise, it could have been considered unfair to Joyner.

Several longtime lawyers in Washington told CNN last week they hadn't heard of a situation as embarrassing as this one, though some former prosecutors in DC conceded that every few years, a jury might land upon a piece of evidence that wasn't examined by law enforcement thoroughly enough.

Judge Rudolph Contreras, who presided over the trial, was flabbergasted.

"The Court shares Mr. Joyner's amazement at law enforcement's failure to uncover the Chinese Yuan, note, and powdery substance in the physical evidence," the judge, who has a decade of experience on the bench, wrote in an opinion a few days later.

"Mr. Liolos, who I know is from New York, is probably astonished that any money got past the police department," the judge also said on the bench, referring to John Liolos, one of Joyner's lawyers.

The FBI declined to comment when asked how agents on the case weren't aware of the drugs and money in the pockets.

When asked about how the evidence oversight happened, a spokesperson for the DC US Attorney's Office didn't answer directly.

Prosecutors alleged Joyner had robbed 10 convenience stores and gas stations in central Washington, Maryland and northern Virginia in the spring of 2023. The robberies at first started a few days apart in April, then by May 2, Joyner was hitting several in the same day, they alleged. He also was accused of armed carjackings around two of the days that the armed robberies occurred.

The series of incidents resulted in a 28-count indictment against Joyner in 2023. He wasn't charged with drug possession.

The case was big for the US Attorney's Office. The trial lasted a full month, with the jury hearing witnesses testify over 10 trial days, then deliberations lasting another week. Joyner had as many as nine lawyers and three prosecutors at trial.

As the jury was leaving on July 22, their second day of deliberations, a juror told courthouse staff they had found some items inside a jacket and a sweatshirt found in one of the carjacked cars that had been worn by the alleged robber.

"We were looking at (the jacket), and (one of the jurors) reached in the breast pocket and she pulled out — it looked like a receipt, but there was a white powder or white substance inside," the jury foreperson told the court on July 23, the next morning, according to a trial transcript obtained by CNN.

"Some of it, kind of, spilled out a little bit, but (a juror) put it back in the pocket and we put it back in the bag," the unnamed juror said.

There was a sweatshirt the jurors could examine too as evidence in the jury room. A juror had looked in the pocket there "and he pulled out — it was crumpled up — it was a bill … one of the Chinese Yuan bills," the foreperson then said.

When the jurors found the suspected drugs and money in the pockets at the end of the second day of jury deliberations, the issue opened up major legal questions for Joyner.

Both items of clothing had been key evidence putting Joyner at the scene of two of the May 2 robberies, and were inside the Toyota he was accused of stealing when police captured it a few days later.

Would the jurors be prejudiced against Joyner now? Had the jury finding the suspected drugs corroborated witness testimony from the trial further than what Joyner's defense lawyers anticipated?

The Justice Department argued that a witness testified about Joyner stealing money during the armed robbery of four different convenience stores. At one of the 7-Elevens, a witness said the robber took his wallet, and it had in it a Chinese Yuan from a college study abroad trip.

A cooperator who drove Joyner separately testified Joyner had paid him in drugs the night Joyner allegedly held up a gas station. The jacket with the apparent drugs in the pocket had been worn by the armed robber.

After the discovery in the pockets, Contreras brought each of the jurors into the courtroom one by one.

He told them the Chinese bill and the apparent drugs weren't part of the evidence in the case. The jurors each told the court they could set aside those items in their consideration of the case against Joyner.

They went back to deliberating.

The following Monday — the fifth day of deliberations — the jury had reached another predicament.

They said they realized they couldn't agree on more than half of the charges — representing five of the alleged armed robberies and one carjacking — Joyner faced.

"The jury remains deadlocked on or unable to vote on the remaining 15 counts in this case," they said in a note to the judge. "Our differences are in the areas of what constitutes a reasonable doubt and in how to determine identity beyond a reasonable doubt … In the absence of additional evidence or testimony, we cannot reach verdicts on the remaining 15 counts."

So, Contreras ended deliberations, taking a partial verdict.

The diligence of the jury, unable to come to an agreement on several of the charges against Joyner, echoed an unusual challenge the US Attorney's Office has faced in several other criminal trials this year.

Still, the jury found Joyner guilty of 13 criminal charges, representing an armed robbery in mid-April 2023 in downtown Washington, and four armed robberies and a carjacking on May 2, 2023, in Northwest Washington and Maryland.

"The jury's verdict ensures the defendant will face a 31year mandatory minimum sentence, making the D.C. community safer with this serial robber off the streets," a spokesperson from the US Attorney's Office said about the case.

Joyner's defense attorneys haven't yet appealed his conviction. They declined to comment because a final judgment in the case is not set in stone.

Correction: This story was updated to correct the year Joyner was indicted, which was 2023.

title: TV's 25 best true-crime shows
description: From mind-boggling murder investigations to decade-long scams, there’s no shortage of documentaries about real-life awfulness. We list the most incredible
fullText:
From mind-boggling murder investigations to decade-long scams, there’s no shortage of documentaries about real-life awfulness. We list the most incredible

Since the true-crime explosion a decade ago – kickstarted by Netflix’s Making a Murderer – audiences have been fed a steady small-screen diet of cold-case killings, catfishing scams and creepy cults. And, after years of varying results, Netflix’s latest show, A Toxic Love Story – which recounts how a California couple framed an innocent woman for stalking, intimidation and recruiting men from Craigslist to rape her ex’s new wife – is being billed as a return to true-crime form. But when it comes to similar shows worth your viewing time, what else is up there?

Here’s a selection of the genre’s 25 standout shows and where to watch them – which, let’s face it, is mainly Netflix. Let the boggle-eyed bingeing begin.

Disney+
This ESPN-produced five-parter, which won an Oscar and an Emmy, is the definitive account of the fairytale rise and steep fall of the former NFL running back OJ Simpson. It chronicles the buildup to and fallout from the 1995 trial at which Simpson was accused (and acquitted) of the brutal murders of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ron Goldman. A stunning state-of-the-nation study of race, gender and celebrity.

Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (UK/US/Australia), Foxtel Now (Australia)

An oldie but a goodie. The HBO series remains groundbreaking for reasons we won’t spoil. The film-maker Andrew Jarecki follows Durst, a billionaire New York real estate heir, who is suspected of three murders across 19 years. When Durst agrees to a sit-down interview, it proves to be the biggest miscalculation of his life.

The director Skye Borgman, whose 2017 film Abducted in Plain Sight also merits a watch, keeps the victim front and centre in this jaw-dropper. In 1990, a young woman was found in critical condition at the side of an Oklahoma highway. What begins as an investigation into an apparent hit-and-run soon escalates into a harrowing tale of abduction, abuse and identity fraud.

Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (US/Australia), YouTube TV (US)

People behind bars in Alabama used contraband phones to film the footage and make the calls from which this startling documentary was largely assembled. The result of a six-year investigation by the directors Charlotte Kaufman and Andrew Jarecki (of The Jinx pedigree), it viscerally lays bare the cruelty inflicted on prisoners as they are beaten, abused and even killed by prison guards. It’s a righteous howl of protest about systemic failures.

In 2003, Brian Wells, a pizza delivery man, walked into a Pennsylvania bank with a bomb locked around his neck and demanded $250,000 in cash. He was killed when the device detonated before cops could disarm it. The film-makers Barbara Schroeder and Trey Borzillieri unravel the conspiracy across four episodes, until a climactic revelation flips everything on its head.

Prime Video (UK), HBO Max/YouTube TV (US)

It starts as a HBO film about clowns hired for children’s parties. It soon morphs into a haunting deep dive into the retired New York schoolteacher Arnold Friedman and his 18-year-old son, Jesse. In 1987, the pair were convicted of owning an extensive cache of child sexual abuse images and abusing local boys who took computing classes in their basement.

In 2018, a pregnant woman, Shanann Watts, and her two toddler daughters were murdered in their Colorado home by Shanann’s husband, Chris. Only days before, he had posted smiley family snaps on social media. Via text messages, home videos, Facebook reels and police bodycam footage, the director Jenny Popplewell constructs a digital portrait of domestic tragedy.

HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), Foxtel Now (Australia)

The stranger-than-fiction story of Gypsy Rose Blanchard. From birth, the Missouri girl was in and out of hospital, diagnosed with all manner of debilitating diseases. She used a wheelchair and was tube-fed and shaven-headed due to cancer. Or so everyone thought. When Gypsy Rose learned the truth, she murdered her mother, Clauddine. This compelling film interviews her in prison. She has since been released on parole.

A true-crime phenomenon that doesn’t involve murder. Just don’t Google it first or you may ruin the head-spinning twist. This cleverly crafted film from Skye Borgman (Girl in the Picture) follows a teen couple in small-town Michigan who are relentlessly cyberbullied by an anonymous caller. A community is torn apart by finger-pointing before the culprit is unmasked. Cue your jaw hitting the floor.

The unsolved murder in 1969 of a nun called Catherine Cesnik is the gateway into a panoramic exposé of endemic abuse at the all-girls school in Baltimore where she taught. Was Sister Cathy killed by a priest when she tried to blow the whistle? This searing seven-parter gives voice to victims, while the lead investigators aren’t journalists but two retired former pupils, working from their kitchen tables.

Those who had followed the tragic case were agog last summer when Bryan Kohberger, accused of fatally stabbing four university housemates in 2022, took a plea deal to avoid the death penalty. Directors Liz Garbus and Matthew Galkin rushed to update their forensic four-parter, which follows not just the investigation but the impact of social media sleuths. A second season is in the works.

Along with The Jinx, which was released months earlier, this is the one that began the true-crime boom. The directors Laura Ricciardi and Moira Demos spent a decade immersed in the case of Steven Avery and Brendan Dassey, Avery’s teenage nephew and alleged accomplice, to build a genre-defining masterpiece. Hard-hitting and heartbreaking, it sparked national outrage and a presidential petition demanding justice.

HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), YouTube TV (US), Foxtel Now (Australia)

The crime author Michelle McNamara spent years obsessively hunting the Golden State Killer – a nocturnal home invader responsible for at least 50 rapes and 13 murders in California in the 1970s and 1980s. This HBO series from Liz Garbus (One Night in Idaho) weaves together the manhunt with a profile of McNamara, who died before the bogeyman was caught at last.

Another Garbus-directed banger – less a whodunnit, more a look at how the legal system values certain lives above others. She spent nearly a decade researching the Gilgo Beach killings, in which more than a dozen women, many of them sex workers, were murdered between 1993 and 2011. Garbus shows empathy for the victims and ​illustrates how those left behind built a supportive community from their shared pain. In June, Rex Heuermann pleaded guilty to seven murders and admitted to an eighth; he was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

When the eccentric novelist Michael Peterson called 911 in 2001 and said his wife, Kathleen, had died after drunkenly falling down the stairs of their North Carolina mansion, he was soon arrested for murder. For this Canal+ (and latterly Netflix) series, the director Jean-Xavier de Lestrade was embedded with Peterson’s defence team, capturing the courtroom drama up close as he defended the charges. In 2017, Peterson entered an Alford plea to voluntary manslaughter, maintaining his innocence but agreeing there was enough evidence to result in a guilty verdict. Not to be confused with the 2022 HBO dramatisation starring Colin Firth and Toni Collette.

This BBC three-parter tells the devastating story of Jean O’Brien and her daughter Megan Bhari, who set up a charity for terminally ill children in 2012 after Bhari was diagnosed with a brain tumour at 13. Other parents started to question O’Brien’s claims about her daughter’s condition, while funds raised for Believe in Magic – including millions from the boyband One Direction – went unaccounted for.

In 1981, the utopian Rajneesh cult – led by the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, AKA Osho – established itself on a ranch in rural Oregon. Three years later, its followers committed the first and biggest bioterrorist attack in US history. This mesmerising, Emmy-winning series interviews perplexed locals and Ma Anand Sheela, formerly a PA to Osho, who died unrepentant in 1990.

Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (UK, US), YouTube TV (US), Binge (Australia)

In the early 90s, the serial killer Richard Rogers – AKA the Last Call Killer – murdered and dismembered four gay men on the east coast of the US. The case was covered by the media in a sensationalist, homophobic style, while the justice system failed the victims; Anthony Caronna’s infuriating but ultimately redemptive series humanises them at last. Each of the four episodes is dedicated to one of the men killed.

We all know the enraging story by now, but this gut-punch series about the notorious sex trafficker – based on James Patterson’s book – lays bare the human tragedy behind the headlines. The director, Lisa Bryant, hears the candid testimony of survivors, including Virginia Giuffre and Maria Farmer, along with former members of Epstein’s staff and the police who investigated his exploitative empire.

Geeta Gandbhir’s unflinching documentary investigates the fatal shooting of a Black Florida woman, Ajike Owens, by her white neighbour, Susan Louise Lorincz. Comprised mostly of police bodycam and interrogation footage, it builds into a searing indictment of community tensions, the state’s controversial “stand your ground” law and systemic racial bias.

In 1993, the murders and mutilation of three eight-year-old boys in Arkansas sparked a moral panic about heavy metal and satanic rituals, resulting in the wrongful arrests of three teenagers. Paradise Lost: The Child Murders at Robin Hood Hills remains the only docuseries for which Metallica have allowed their music to be used. Two sequels followed the case’s progress over the next 15 years.

HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), YouTube TV (US), Spectrum (US), Foxtel Now (Australia)

Nxivm styled itself as a global self-improvement organisation. Of course, it was a cult – one that abused, blackmailed and branded its female members. Its svengali-like leader, Keith Raniere, was ultimately convicted of charges including sex trafficking and racketeering. This unsettling HBO docuseries began filming inside Nxivm years before the FBI investigated, capturing the mechanism of manipulation in action.

Reminiscent of the Zodiac Killer in 1960s San Francisco, Richard Ramirez terrorised Los Angeles in the summer of 1985 with a string of brutal, seemingly random murders and sexual assaults. This four-parter documents his deadly rampage through the lens of the two detectives, Gil Carrillo and Frank Salerno, who became consumed by the case and doggedly tracked him down.

“Hey, all you cool cats and kittens.” It’s now inextricably linked with the early months of the Covid pandemic, but if this talking-point series managed to escape you, it’s worth seeing what all the fuss was about. Investigative film-making with the pull of reality trash, it follows an eccentric Oklahoma zookeeper, Joe Exotic, who allegedly hired a hitman to kill a big-cat activist, Carole Baskin.

A twisting, turning thriller with the kicker that it’s all too real. This three-parter beggars belief as it follows Facebook sleuths who launch an amateur investigation into online videos of kitten cruelty. The armchair detectives repeatedly express their fears that the culprit will escalate to murdering more than just pets – and are proved correct.

fullText:
A man charged with starting one of the wildfires in Spokane, Washington, that have destroyed hundreds of buildings planned the crime for weeks and researched when the weather would be best for igniting it, police said.

Aaron Farinacci expressed that "fire is powerful, beautiful, and that things that go through fire experience a kind of rebirth," Spokane County Detective Michael Drapeau said in a court filing Wednesday, recalling his interview with him.

Farinacci, 37, is charged with starting the Old Trails Fire, one of three fires in the Spokane area that have burned more than 850 homes and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people. He is also charged in connection with two smaller fires ignited in the summer of 2025.

He was scheduled to be arraigned on three first-degree arson charges Thursday, but his lawyer asked for a competency evaluation before he enters a plea. Spokane Superior Court Judge Jeremy Schmidt said he would review that request. He set bond for $2 million, ruling that Farinacci was a risk to community safety, a flight risk and that there was potential for a violent offense.

Defense attorney Colin Charbonneau did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Farinacci denied starting the fire when police initially contacted him, but during an interview with Drapeau, he confessed to the current fire as well as others last year. That led to the two additional arson charges.

He told the detective that he always carries marijuana or cigarettes so he would have a legitimate reason to have a lighter and matches.

"He knows arson is an easy crime to get away from if you have time, and he had time," Drapeau said.

Farinacci researched the weather to predict a day that would have "high winds, low humidity, sort of high heat" for starting the Old Trails Fire, Drapeau said. He also looked up the work of a well-known serial arsonist and purchased items to make a "time delay device" for igniting a wildfire, using notebook paper, matches, a cigarette and a rubber band, the detective said.

Farinacci picked Saturday, Aug. 1, to start the fire because he knew there would be strong winds — reaching 50 mph (80 kph), the detective said.

Farinacci said he knew it "'was gonna get bad,'" the detective said, but Farinacci claimed he didn't intend it to grow as much as it did.

Paul Child, 64, has been credited with leading police to Farinacci. He was driving with his grandson along some railroad tracks when he saw a man standing there and looking toward nearby trees. About 10 minutes later, the man was still there.

"He was bent over in the brush, acting nervous," Child told The Associated Press on Tuesday. "You get the feeling this guy's up to something."

Drapeau said Farinacci also admitted responsibility for 25 fires near his apartment building in summer 2025. Most were near the Spokane River or the Centennial Trail.

Farinacci said he didn't think the Aubrey White Fire that ignited on July 6, 2025, would cause damage but "one house got 'slightly damaged' from the side," the detective said. That blaze started near the Centennial Trail and soon became a large wildfire that threatened homes and structures, the court filing said. It led to evacuations and road closures. An investigation determined it was caused by arson, but police didn't have any suspects.

The Aubrey White Fire was added to the charges against Farinacci, as was the Meenach Fire, the court filing states.

Farinacci served about a decade in prison after killing his father in Mesa, Arizona, in 2010. He also shot himself at that time but survived. He was charged with murder but pleaded guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault. Farinacci's lawyer repeatedly raised concerns about his mental health during the case.

Drapeau said Farinacci indicated that he moved to the Copper River Apartments in the Spokane area in October 2022.

A son was born in 2025 and "he began having trouble dealing with life issues," the detective said. "He began smoking marijuana at about this time."

title: Ukraine accuses Russia of war crime after video shows drone attacking vegetable seller in Kherson
description: KYIV, Aug 4 () - Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern Ukrainian city of K...
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson.

Footage released by Ukrainian police ‌shows the drone pursuing a man around a van being used as a street stand before exploding as he dives for ‌cover behind the vehicle. Police said the man in his 50s survived but suffered shock and shrapnel injuries.

Ukrainian officials later identified him only as a 52-year-old called Yurii and released ​a video interview with him from a hospital ward.

"Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone 'safari' Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy wrote on X, saying that "Russia has gone mad" and calling for more pressure on Moscow and strong security guarantees for Ukraine.

"We must act and support life in ways that force Russia to think seriously about peace rather than expanding the range of its drones."

Russia's Defence Ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters request for comment ⁠on the incident.

The vegetable seller went to Kherson in the morning to sell produce, said Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration. Prokudin released the video interview with the man on the Telegram app.

"I only just put up the umbrella and started unloading the boxes. My wife was there, ​too. ​Then we heard it buzzing but could not even see it. It came ​from somewhere behind the market, from those bushes over there, ‌and flew in very low," said Yurii, sitting in a hospital ward.

"It is open steppe. There is nowhere to go. It is terrifying, of course. Really terrifying."

On the video, Yurii showed his wounds on both legs and also on his back. His wife ran off and was not injured, he said.

Sybiha said the attack formed part of a deliberate Russian campaign to intimidate civilians. "This barbaric Russian war crime in Kherson demands international condemnation and justice, but thousands of similar crimes never come to the public eye," he wrote on Telegram.

In July, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission ‌in Ukraine said it had documented 1,396 civilian deaths and 7,978 injuries in ​the first six months of 2026, marking a 37% increase from 2025 and more than ​double the figures from 2024.

It said that the surge in ​civilian casualties was primarily driven by intensifying Russian long-range missile and drone strikes targeting cities far from the front ‌lines.

Ukraine is also attacking Russia with drones and long-range missiles, ​many of which have caused civilian ​casualties, Russian authorities say.

Russia on Monday accused Ukraine of terrorism after seven people, including three children, were killed at its Black Sea holiday resort of Gelendzhik in what it said was a deliberate Ukrainian drone attack on civilians.

A Ukrainian official said that the drone ​only fell on the beach in Gelendzhik because ‌it was shot down by Russian air defences, adding that "Ukraine uses its weapons exclusively against the Russian military-industrial complex and economic ​infrastructure facilities".

Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians in the war triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

(Reporting ​by Aleksandar Vasovic, Olena Harmash; Editing by Ros Russell and Hugh Lawson)

title: Devastated mother blames soft-on-crime policies after career criminal is charged in son’s death
description: Jacob Freytes' family pushes for mandatory life sentences for child killers after the 12-year-old was fatally struck by a stray bullet in the Bronx.
fullText:
The family of a 12-year-old boy killed by a stray bullet in the Bronx is demanding change after a suspect with a lengthy arrest record was charged with his murder.

After the death of Jacob Freytes, the son of a retired NYPD detective sergeant, his mother and sister are pushing for "Jacob's Law," which they say would require life sentences for people convicted of recklessly taking a child's life.

"I gave him a kiss, and I walked out, and we always do a little dolphin kiss. And I walked out and went to work," Migdalia Martinez, Freytes' mother, told "Fox & Friends" Tuesday.

2 Detained After Shooting In New York Leaves 15-Year-old Killed, Two Others Wounded: Police

"Around five o'clock, they called me and said that he had gotten shot. And all I could do was try to think of different ways to get here faster," she added. "When I got there, I just seen my boy gone."

Freytes, who was riding his bike to a nearby bodega to buy a ball, was shot and killed after a suspect opened fire during an alleged street dispute. Two other adults were also wounded in the shooting.

Police said William Ferrer, 45, was arrested and faces multiple charges, including second-degree murder. He has pleaded not guilty. Ferrer has an arrest record dating back more than 25 years, including prior charges for drunk driving, drug possession, menacing and criminal contempt, according to the New York Post.

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch addressed Ferrer's arrest on X, writing, "Jacob was an innocent bystander on his bike when he was taken from his family yesterday in an act of senseless gun violence.

House Democrat Blasted After Early Release Law Freed Inmates Later Charged With Murder

"No arrest can ever ease the pain of this unimaginable loss, but the NYPD will continue to do everything in our power to seek justice for Jacob."

The family is calling for a proposed "Jacob's Law" that they say would require life sentences for people convicted of recklessly taking a child's life. The family also criticized New York's crime policies, including cash bail reforms for misdemeanors and the end of stop-and-frisk.

"It's just so much that they allow that, at this point, it's just safer more for the criminals than it is for hardworking people," Martinez said.

Freytes' sister, Angelica Coriano, said the family welcomed the charges but remained uneasy about whether the suspect would receive enough prison time if convicted.

Louisiana Bill Expands First-degree Murder Charges And Death Penalty Eligibility After Mall Shooting

"'Jacob's Law' will allow for there to be no in-between whether somebody goes to jail or not for taking a child's life recklessly. It'll allow for criminals to go straight to jail or prison instead of the family having to go to court continuously hoping and wondering if they're [going to] get the justice that they deserve for the child that they lost," Coriano said.

"And we went to court and found out all the charges that he'd be receiving, which is great, but we still have to sit with the worry whether he'll face all the time that is necessary enough to keep him where he needs to be. And that type of uncertainty is very uncomfortable for us as a family, knowing that we'll never see our child again."

Martinez remembered her son as a "funny, quirky kid" who loved his friends, family and playing video games.

"There wasn't an old woman he didn't help with bags or cross the street," she said. "There wasn't a person that if he caught your eye, he'd make sure to tell you hi."

title: Attorney who defended DC sniper says Kohberger faces 'monumental uphill battle' undoing guilty plea
description: A criminal defense attorney explains why Bryan Kohberger's effort to undo his University of Idaho murders guilty plea faces two significant legal hurdles.
fullText:
Bryan Kohberger faces a "monumental uphill battle" in his effort to withdraw his guilty plea in the murders of four University of Idaho students, according to an attorney who represented D.C. sniper Lee Boyd Malvo and once helped another client successfully withdraw a guilty plea before winning an acquittal.

Mark Petrovich, who represented Malvo in post-conviction proceedings in Virginia and has decades of criminal defense experience, told Fox News Digital that defendants rarely succeed in withdrawing guilty pleas after sentencing, even in cases involving claims that they were unaware of potentially exculpatory evidence before entering the plea.

He cautioned against drawing direct comparisons between Malvo's post-conviction litigation and Kohberger's effort to withdraw his guilty plea. Malvo's appeals stemmed from changes in constitutional law governing juvenile sentencing, while Kohberger is attempting to undo a plea agreement he entered as an adult after avoiding the death penalty.

Kaylee Goncalves' Mother Says Family Ready For Trial After Bryan Kohberger Seeks To Withdraw Guilty Plea

"It's a monumental uphill battle," Petrovich said. "First of all, getting the judge to allow you to withdraw the plea, and then second of all to winning any new proceeding, because there's a lot against you."

Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to the stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves in Moscow, Idaho, in November 2022. He was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after accepting a plea agreement that spared him from the death penalty.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

In recent court filings, Kohberger claimed he was pressured into accepting the plea agreement, did not fully understand potentially exculpatory evidence before pleading guilty and was misled about the conditions he would face while incarcerated.

Idaho Murders: New Book On Kohberger Reveals Previously Unseen Evidence, Claims Sheath Could Be Inadmissible

He contends those factors undermined the voluntariness of his decision to plead guilty.

Petrovich said he once represented a client who sought to withdraw a guilty plea before sentencing. A judge granted the request, the case proceeded to trial and the client was acquitted, but he said Kohberger's circumstances are fundamentally different because he has already been sentenced.

"You can't wait until after you're sentenced and see what the consequences of the plea are and then change your plea," Petrovich said. "It's going to be a very, very difficult burden to overcome."

Alex Murdaugh Murder Saga Lands Right Back Where It Started Before Next Lowcountry Courtroom Battle

Petrovich said Kohberger would face two significant hurdles even if a judge allowed him to withdraw his plea.

One would be convincing jurors after previously admitting guilt under oath.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Even if a judge allowed Kohberger to withdraw his plea, Petrovich said jurors would almost certainly learn he had already admitted guilt, creating another significant obstacle at trial.

"One thing that's important is that you still can't hide from the jury the fact that you said under oath that you're guilty," Petrovich said. "Even if you withdraw, then you have to explain that ... if you're going to get anywhere with any kind of jury finding."

Petrovich also questioned whether Kohberger's attorneys would have advised him to accept a plea agreement without first reviewing the evidence disclosed during discovery.

He noted that defense attorneys handling capital cases typically spend years reviewing discovery before recommending whether a client should plead guilty.

"The attorneys on the case ... were intimately familiar with the evidence and the information that was provided to them by law enforcement and prosecution," Petrovich said. "I'm sure they knew all about everything. If they encouraged him or if there was a discussion and a plea was decided on, I'm sure it was for good reason."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Kohberger's case is not the first involving a notorious killer who later sought to undo a guilty plea.

James Earl Ray pleaded guilty in 1969 to assassinating the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to avoid a potential death sentence. Three days after entering his guilty plea, Ray sought to withdraw it, arguing he had been pressured into confessing. He spent the rest of his life trying to undo the plea but died in prison in 1998 without ever receiving the jury trial he sought.

Serial killer Clifton Bloomfield unsuccessfully sought to withdraw guilty pleas after admitting to five murders in New Mexico to avoid capital punishment. Washington serial killer Robert Lee Yates Jr. also challenged his plea agreement after admitting to murdering 13 women, but courts ultimately rejected both efforts.

Kohberger's plea agreement spared him from facing a capital trial and ended years of pretrial litigation in one of the country's most closely watched murder prosecutions.

Petrovich said that history, combined with the years of discovery and plea negotiations leading up to Kohberger's agreement, makes the effort to withdraw it especially difficult.

title: Gang of men hurl racist abuse at takeaway owner before violent attack
description: The BBC understands police are treating the attack in Falkirk last month as a hate crime.
fullText:
A business owner has said that a group of men hurled racist abuse at him before punching him and smashing his head into a wall in the street in Falkirk.

Dr Zohaib Arshad said the group approached him on Grahams Road last month when he was visiting one of his takeaway shops and asked him when he was "leaving the country" before launching the unprovoked attack.

The 39-year-old, who practised as a vet in Pakistan, patched himself up with glue stitches rather than wait at A&E. He said his children are now fearful of being attacked in school.

BBC Scotland understands the police are treating the incident as a hate crime.

A spokesperson for the force said inquiries into the attack are ongoing.

Arshad stood as an Alba Party candidate for Falkirk at the 2024 General Election and is now a member of the SNP.

His political connections have resulted in the issue being brought to the attention of the Scottish Parliament - however he fears it would have gone unnoticed had he been any other member of the public.

More stories from Tayside and Central

Listen to news from Tayside and Central on BBC Sounds

Arshad said he had just parked his car and was walking to one of his shops on the evening of Monday 20 July.

He said: "Two or three guys approached me and said 'when are you leaving the country by the way?'"

The businessman said he tried to walk away but one of the group banged his head into the wall.

"I had blood all over my face and in my eyes and when I was cleaning up the blood from my eyes one of the guys punched me on my head a few times," he said.

He told how he then ended up in a fight with one of the men as he tried to defend himself, and that the man threatened to stab him.

Despite there being lots of people around, he said nobody came to his assistance.

"Everybody got their phone at that time instead of helping me or helping that guy to take the situation out. Everybody was just filming us," he said.

The 39-year-old said that after calling the police it took 45 minutes for officers to arrive, by which time the men had left the scene.

When Arshad called for an ambulance, he claims he was told to make his own way to A&E.

"I called A&E and A&E said oh it's 14 hours to get the stitches," he said.

He feared that leaving the wound untreated for that long would leave him with a worse scar, so called some of his friends who work in medicine to see if they had "glue stitches at home" and stitched the wound up in "the back of the shop".

Following the attack, Arshad said his family are "terrified" and he is being "much more vigilant".

"My wee boy, he's nine and said 'dad, if I go to school, can they do it to me as well?'"

He added that despite his wife and his mother urging him to move to France where he lived previously, he has no plans to leave Scotland.

"We cannot leave anything just because of one bad person - defeat is not an option," he said.

It comes at a time of heightened tension over the issue of immigration in Scotland.

Police made several arrests in the opening weekend of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow after masked demonstrators rampaged through the city and targeted people for the colour of their skin.

Earlier in the day a peaceful anti-racism protest had been taking place at Glasgow Green before anti-immigration protesters arrived at the same location - police estimated 1,700 people had attended.

Later that day a group marching through the city shouted racist abuse and hurled a traffic cone at a delivery driver who was picking up an order.

A video of the attack on Muhammad Jawad Yaqoob circulated on social media - it shows a number of young men shouting "get them out" before one throws the orange cone. They cheer as Yaquoob runs away from them into a nearby restaurant.

Police Scotland said it was investigating the incident.

title: Police in the US are making their own true crime podcasts
description: More police departments are trying to invigorate unsolved murder or missing cases through the power of podcasts.
fullText:
Peter Chadwick had been on the run for nearly four years, charged with murdering his wife, when California police launched a podcast about the crime.

He was captured in Mexico 10 months and 20 days later.

Karen Schepers had been missing for more than four decades when another police force, in Illinois, debuted the first episode of a podcast last year about the cold case - and her body was found at the bottom of a river within weeks.

Now Colorado investigators are hoping to bring in elusive tips about a 10-year-old unsolved murder, too. The Aurora Police Department (APD) released its own podcast this summer in an attempt to achieve justice for Chelsea Yasser, 21, who was found fatally stabbed in a shopping centre parking lot in 2016.

As the barrelling behemoth of true crime content continues to flourish, police departments across the US and abroad are turning to podcast production for help solving cold murder cases and other investigations.

"The true crime genre - whether it's TV, whether it's podcasts, whether it's books – I mean, it's wildly popular," says Joe Moylan, Aurora Police Department's public information officer. "And we absolutely were deliberate in trying to tap into that broader audience."

The phenomenon is still in its infancy and brings its own benefits and pitfalls - but experts believe the trend will grow.

"I think it's a tool that everyone will eventually embrace," says Michael Alcazar, retired NYPD detective and adjunct professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. True crime podcasts can air inaccurate information, he says, but this way police get to control what is out there and seek new tip-offs.

There were already plenty of podcasts featuring former detectives discussing cases or policing issues, says Alyce McGovern, associate professor in criminology at University of New South Wales in Australia, where law enforcement has also begun dipping its toes into podcast production.

But it's rarer for police department-produced podcasts to focus on cold cases and solicit tips, as the California, Colorado and Illinois departments have done.

The police programmes are episodic in nature, outlining the crimes, victims and investigations with narrative panache and interesting details - much the same way that groundbreaking true crime podcast Serial did when it debuted in 2014.

In Aurora, police hoped to produce a podcast that was equally engaging - and would prompt listeners to come forward with any relevant information.

The killing of Chelsea Yasser has been described by the podcasters as the "White Whale", of Moby Dick fame, given how long it has haunted investigators.

Yasser was fatally stabbed after getting into a minivan that pulled up in the parking lot; she collapsed moments after leaving the vehicle. Grainy surveillance footage captured the rocking van as the assault took place, but the images were not clear enough to discern a face and DNA recovered from under her fingernails matched no one in the system.

As the APD released the podcast in June, detectives were testing the DNA using new forensic genealogy technology, and the programme updated listeners about other new lines of enquiry.

The department has issued appeals for information on the Yasser murder before, but the podcast can cast a far wider net for witnesses and tipsters, Moylan says.

"If you weren't watching the news that night when it happened, or if you didn't pick up a newspaper, you might not know anything about this case, so we wanted to tap into that broader audience.

"Assuming that the suspect is still alive and out there somewhere, they could be anywhere in the country."

The podcast had been downloaded 7,184 times by the end of July, according to APD - yielding several tips, including one which investigators continue to pursue.

Most departments don't have the staff, budget or time needed to produce podcast content, nor do they have the equipment or expertise.

Others hold off for fear of repercussions, lawsuits and civil liability, says retired detective Alcazar.

In California, Newport Beach Police Department's podcast about the fugitive Chadwick, for example, was not without controversy. The millionaire was introduced to viewers in Episode 1 as "a man who killed his wife in the peaceful coastal community of Newport Beach, California in October 2012".

Chadwick had been charged and pleaded not guilty, but not tried - yet the podcast made no use of the word "alleged" and called the millionaire a "murderer". Critics argued that it flew in the face of innocent-before-proven-guilty parameters and that the job of police was to investigate, not adjudicate.

The podcast was produced and hosted by public information officer Jennifer Manzella, who defended the choice at the time, saying police "put out the same kinds of statements all the time".

She tells BBC News that she was trying to balance telling the story in an engaging way without jeopardising the investigation.

After Chadwick's August 2019 apprehension, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison - where he remains.

Manzella says it wasn't a direct tip from the podcast that led to his capture - but it undeniably helped because it put pressure on Chadwick while on the run, making him more likely to make mistakes.

And investigators were able to obtain warrants and extraditions "in record time" because of the awareness - the podcast hit Number 24 on the iTunes chart.

In the wake of the podcast - and Chadwick's capture - she got calls from other departments and agencies interested in producing something similar.

But not everyone has been behind the idea.

"I initially was not really interested in it," says Detective Andrew Houghton - and now podcast co-host - at Elgin Police Department in Illinois. He worked on Elgin's 2025 podcast Somebody Knows Something alongside Detective Matthew Vartarian with assistance from a local radio station.

Houghton and Vartarian had just been assigned to Elgin's new cold case unit in 2024 when the chief informed them that the job would also involve podcasting.

"We're already starting this new unit," Houghton recalls. "Why are we adding something else new on top of that?"

Houghton and his partner begrudgingly began figuring out how to arrange episodes and soon discovered the process was also helping them structure the investigation. They formed different theories about what had happened to the missing 23-year-old, and each theory naturally formed an episode.

The podcast not only generated tips but also gave the detectives more ways to find leads. They started going through posts on social media about their own programme.

"They'd say, like, 'Oh, my mom worked with this person, or I live in this neighbourhood and I remember this.'"

The detectives ultimately solved the case through old-fashioned policework; one of their theories had been that Schepers had crashed her car and ended up in the river.

They had found a 1999 local newspaper story claiming that police had searched salvage yards by helicopter as well as dragging the Fox River but there was no evidence the latter had happened. And they did not shy away from telling listeners this.

So the department brought in a search company with the latest sonar technology as well as divers - and they found Schepers and her car at the bottom of the river in March 2025.

Now they're on the third season of the podcast. They shook up the format for the second, focusing on homicides, but have returned to a missing persons case.

Houghton acknowledges that "it is a lot of work - it takes a lot of time and effort".

As other departments navigate those budgetary and resource issues, however, there's a consensus that podcasts as an investigative tool will be seen more frequently.

If police departments can find the staffing to sustain it, podcasting could help in both recruitment and staff retention, says Janice Iwama, associate professor in American University's department of justice, law and criminology. It gives listeners the chance to learn more about what policing is really like, from the mouths of working officers.

Generational change could also fuel the trend, says retired NYPD Detective Alcazar, because younger police officers will be more ready to embrace the opportunities presented by podcasts and social media.

"That's their world," he says. "That's what they're most comfortable with."

fullText:
Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’

A high-profile publishing deal for a debut crime novel has collapsed after doubts emerged over whether artificial intelligence played a role in writing it.

The hotly anticipated manuscript Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body, by Jerry Falade, was withdrawn from sale by its agent despite reportedly receiving an offer for more than $2m (£1.5m) from Minotaur, owned by Macmillan US, as part of a 14-way auction. The plan was to publish it in 2028.

An email sent to publishers by Falade’s agents and seen by the Guardian said: “Jerry Falade produced an incredible manuscript that dazzled us and the top publishing professionals around the world. Unfortunately, we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion.”

It continued: “During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with Jerry for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilising AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book.”

The US auction was run by the author’s agent Marc Gerald of Europa Content, according to the Bookseller. In the UK, Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary is said to have secured several six-figure bids through a similarly competitive process. The Guardian has approached both agents for comment.

Gerald told the Bookseller he first read the book in June, and that it was “stunningly good, everyone fell in love with it. It’s a book that appeals to absolutely everyone.”

He said that halfway through the submissions process, an editor raised concerns that the book had signs of potential AI use. Gerald said Europa opted against using AI-detection software to check the manuscript, saying Falade was “clear and credible” in his explanation.

However, after a meeting on 29 July, when “aspects of [Falade’s] story changed”, the agency decided to cut ties, citing the “need to have total faith”.

“We feel terrible for putting this into the universe and the firestorm it has caused,” Gerald added. “The book itself is genius – however it came to be drafted, it’s amazing.”

Falade’s case is the latest in a string of controversies to hit publishing this year, as authors, agents and publishers grapple with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts. Earlier this year, Hachette pulled the US release of Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl after rumours circulated online that the author had relied on AI, something she denies.

In a statement to the Guardian, Falade rejected claims that he had used AI and said the response reflected racial bias in publishing.

He said: “Three Black authors received major publishing deals this year, and all three later had deals cancelled or disrupted following suspicions about AI. There seems to be a troubling assumption that when a Black writer produces work that attracts significant attention, the work could not possibly be their own. Meanwhile, there are popular white writers who have publicly mentioned using AI for their writing processes and they’re still doing fine.”

Falade did not name other authors, but two Black authors in the US – Ballard and HM Wolfe, author of the viral romance Daggermouth – faced allegations of AI use this year. Wolfe also denies she used AI.

Falade said: “In my case, rumours began circulating and, within six hours, I had been dropped by my agency, deals were paused, and press releases were being issued.” He added that AI-detection tools “are widely known to produce false positives”. He said the novel had “passed through first readers, second readers, editors, and acquisitions teams at numerous publishing houses … If the manuscript had shown genuine signs of being generated by AI, it is difficult to believe that every one of those experienced professionals would have failed to notice.”

title: Trump’s Caribbean Killing Spree Is a Feckless, Criminal Failure
description: Jeet...
fullText:
Blowing up innocent fishermen hasn’t curbed the drug trade.

On January 19, Carlos Mero, the captain of an Ecuadoran fishing boat named La Fiorella, called his wife on an emergency line and expressed his alarm at seeing “American aircraft, two drones, and a blue patrol ship” nearby. Mero was right to be worried. Starting in the fall of 2025, the Trump administration, on the pretense of waging a war on drugs, had ramped up a military campaign to bomb supposed drug-running boats in the Caribbean and Pacific—often in concert with regional allies such as Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa. Mero was baffled as to why his boat was seemingly under the gunsight of the US military, since La Fiorella had been inspected and cleared by a local coast guard.

As Drop Site News reported, witnesses saw La Fiorella explode the next day. Its eight crew members, including Mero, all disappeared. There is still no confirmation that the boat was targeted by the US military, but the facts of the case are in keeping with the more than 60 boats in the Caribbean that have been bombed, which have left at least 221 dead (a number that does include probable but unverified kills such as La Fiorella).

Other examples of US-sponsored extrajudicial killing were recently highlighted in a report by Human Rights Watch. According to the organization, the report documents

serious human rights violations in a rural community on the Colombia-Ecuador border, as well as attacks on and the disappearance of fishermen at sea near the Galápagos Islands. Each incident either clearly implicates the US-Ecuador security partnership or surfaces questions about responsibility. Ecuadorian forces tortured and arbitrarily detained four farm workers, and later burned and struck a dairy farm, during what the United States called a “partnered operation.” And drones of unknown origin attacked two fishing vessels, injuring several crew members. A third vessel remains missing.

Donald Trump is inordinately proud of his intensification of the war on drugs, which he’s touted as a great success. In a Truth Social post in April, Trump claimed, “98.2% of Drugs coming into the U.S. by Ocean or Sea have STOPPED!” Quoting Trump’s words, The Washington Post reports, “Trump has said at least 15 times, including as recently as last month, that the strikes have reduced maritime drug trafficking into the country by 97 or 98 percent.”

Any sentient creature will be skeptical of Trump’s claim since he has a long history of outrageous and completely divorced from reality lying. But it’s worth noting that even if Trump’s claims were true, they would not in fact justify the US killing spree. Smuggling drugs is a crime, not an act of war that merits summary execution. As I’ve noted before, Trump’s policy is a war crime, full stop.

But as it turns out, these war crimes are as ineffectual as they are vile. On Monday, the Post reported:

The Trump administration’s deadly military strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats have not reduced the amount of cocaine entering the United States, but they’re prompting criminal organizations to develop new strategies and tactics and undermining traditional investigative methods, according to a previously unreported assessment by the Drug Enforcement Administration, a closed-door congressional briefing and interviews with current and former U.S. and foreign officials.

In a recent assessment reviewed by The Washington Post, DEA analysts found the strikes had failed to affect the supply or price of cocaine in the United States and had led traffickers to diversify beyond go-fast boats and to avoid international waters, opting instead for larger boats and hemming close to coastlines, where U.S. forces are less likely to open fire. In a closed-door briefing last month, Pentagon officials told lawmakers the strikes in international waters off South and Central America had not reduced its purity.

This was an entirely predictable fiasco. The War on Drugs has been a bipartisan effort dating back to the Nixon administration. The simplest way to document its failure is to note that during this period, the price of drugs that are regarded as most dangerous has continued a long-term decline. In 2012, the price of cocaine was 80 percent less than in 1982. According to the Post, “Based on pricing, there might, in fact, now be more cocaine circulating in the United States. In Florida, cocaine is selling for $13,000 to $15,000 per kilogram, a senior DEA official said, a drop of roughly 50 percent over the last five years.”

The War on Drugs might in fact be the only effective anti-inflation policy the United States has ever developed. While nearly everything else, ranging from food to housing to transportation, gets more costly, it has never been cheaper to get high as a kite. This is true no matter how many innocent fishermen the United States military drops bombs on or how many Central and South American governments get trained in the dark art of torture. The drug issue is driven by supply more than demand. As long as people in the United States have an inordinate interest in drugs, drugs will be extremely profitable, which means that smugglers will find ever-more-ingenious ways to get their goods to the market.

Trump’s escalation of the War on Drugs is vile, but it reflects a deeper failure in the US political system. Trump isn’t the only one who has failed to learn that the War on Drugs is lost. On this issue, at least, he is merely building on a long and discredited tradition.

title: LA real estate vet comes at Mayor Bass with receipts over damning homelessness report: 'She doesn't get it'
description: John Alle says Mayor Karen Bass has repeatedly refused invitations to tour LA neighborhoods plagued by crime, drug use and rising street homelessness.
fullText:
LOS ANGELES, CA – As new data show homelessness rising in Los Angeles, local activist John Alle said Mayor Karen Bass has neglected her responsibility to address the issue and witness firsthand the crime, drug use and deteriorating conditions in some of the city's hardest-hit neighborhoods.

The Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority released its 2026 annual homeless count Friday, finding overall homelessness increased 3.4% in LA and 1.2% across the Los Angeles Continuum of Care following two consecutive years of declines, though LAHSA said "neither change is considered statistically significant."

The count estimated 45,194 people were experiencing homelessness in LA and 73,040 across the Continuum of Care, which excludes Long Beach, Pasadena and Glendale.

"She doesn't get it. She doesn't see it," John Alle, a Santa Monica business owner and co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition who owns properties across Los Angeles, told Fox News Digital in an interview last month.

Karen Bass Grilled Over Broken Homelessness Promise, Blames Bureaucracy For Slowed Progress

"We've invited her numerous times to ride along with us through Alvarado, Third Street, Park View, MacArthur Park and Westlake. Come drive with us. Have a police officer follow behind for security. And she refused."

The report also found street homelessness rose 7.9% in Los Angeles and 3.3% countywide, with an estimated 29,115 people living on the streets in the city. LAHSA said funding cuts affecting Time-Limited Subsidies and other economic factors reduced the number of people permanently housed by about 5,100 from the "record high of 28,625 people housed permanently in 2024."

In a press release Thursday responding to the data, Bass argued funding cuts "at the federal and state levels" contributed to the rise, adding the Trump administration had "driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and rent — pushing more families to the edge — and slashed critical safety net funding."

"For two years straight, we drove down homelessness by historic margins — but as expected, last year our efforts ultimately couldn't keep up with policies and funding cuts at the federal and state levels that pushed more people onto the streets," she said.

Bass also admitted in a May interview with CNN's Elex Michaelson that she did not fulfill her promise to end street homelessness in the city by 2026 because she "didn't anticipate some of the bureaucratic barriers" her administration would face.

Alle said crime has "gotten so bad" in neighborhoods including Little Bangladesh, which Bass has previously described as one of "LA's most vibrant communities."

"In Little Bangladesh, the crime is so bad that we're finding people on the streets unconscious," he said. "We're having handymen pick up needles and dispose of them."

Spencer Pratt Says His Policy Will Force Homeless Out Of La And Into Cities Like Seattle

Pointing to his tenants' experiences, Alle said he sees the impact of the crisis every day on the "mom-and-pop" renters who live in his apartment buildings and pay thousands of dollars a month, saying "it doesn't sit well with me."

"From people overdosing outside the gated apartment buildings I own, to people attacking each other, murders, and calling 911 only to be put on hold for sometimes an hour, and then being told, 'Well, you're lucky. Sometimes it's two hours,'" he said.

Alle accused Bass of ignoring neighborhood conditions despite living nearby at Getty House, the mayor's official residence in Windsor Square.

"The streetlights are out," he said. "The rubbish isn't collected. The streets are dirty. It's one thing to complain about copper wire theft, but we're just talking about normal streetlights and replacing the bulbs."

But it's not just residents who are affected, according to Alle, who said small businesses are being forced to close early to avoid crime and making it harder to stay in the city.

"When I see them having to leave work at four o'clock, I see them having to close their businesses at four o'clock during the winter and at dusk during the summer," he said. "That's not good. I want them to succeed. If they don't succeed, they can't afford to stay in LA. I feel for them, and their problems are my problems."

Housing First Is A Disaster. I Saw Sacramento's Homeless Chaos Firsthand

Multiple studies have found that a large portion of homeless individuals in Los Angeles County aren't originally from there and Alle has been vocal about how his coalition partnered with an artificial intelligence company to create an AI-powered hotline that has helped more than 40 homeless people return to their home states over the past year.

"They've called us from shelters," he said. "They've called us from parks. The people calling aren't entrenched with the drugs or the gangs. They came here for noble reasons."

Additionally, Alle said his coalition collaborates with local law enforcement, paying for bus, plane or train tickets to help homeless people voluntarily return home, where they can reunite with family or enter treatment programs.

"We're not gonna put them behind the slammer," he said.

Alle said the most "heartbreaking" part is watching families embrace loved ones returning home, with many looking "completely different" after recovery.

"It's a long road ahead, but they're trying because they've seen hell in LA," he said.

While acknowledging the program won't end all homelessness, Alle said helping even a small number of people rebuild their lives is a victory.

"One person saved is great. Fifteen percent, and the 40 people we've saved, is tremendous," he said.

Bass will face off against progressive City Councilwoman Nithya Raman, who has her own ties to the homeless crisis as chair of the Los Angeles City Council's Housing and Homelessness Committee, in her bid to win another term as mayor in November.

title: Burma approves death penalty for scammers months after FBI's $8 billion crypto crackdown

fullText:
Burma's government approved the death penalty as punishment for internet scammers just months after the Fbi announced a sweeping $8 billion crackdown on scam networks coming from the country, according to the country's state-backed media.

The Anti-Online Scam Law passed the country's parliament on Tuesday, green lighting the death penalty for anyone who participates in a scam in which they "commit violence, torture, unlawfully arrest or detain, or treat any person in a cruel manner," according to The Global New Light of Myanmar, a media outlet jointly operated by a private company and the country's Ministry of the Interior.

Burma, also known as Myanmar, has become ground zero for digital scams, with criminals often recruiting migrants from other Asian countries with promises of legitimate work only to imprison them and force them to conduct the scams.

In May, the FBI announced a massive crackdown on a criminal network in Burma known as the "Democratic Karen Benevolent Army." The operation resulted in the seizure of 127,000 Bitcoin, worth over $8 billion as of July.

Fbi Brings Alleged China-linked Hacker To Us In Rare Extradition As Patel Defends Italy Trip

The scammers, who allegedly have ties to Chinese organized crime, had been specifically targeting Americans in their operations, extracting over $3 million from one elderly American, the FBI previously told Fox News Digital.

In 2025, Chinese, Thai and Burmese authorities liberated more than 7,000 people from locked compounds in Burma.

New Germany Sex-crime Figures Reignite Migration Fight As Exploitation Probe Expands

While the new Anti-Online Scam Law only mandates the death penalty for offenses that lead to another person's death, the law mandates 10 years in prison for any instance of forced labor in relation to cybercrime.

The law's approval also comes two days before the United Nations International Organization for Migration's World Day Against Trafficking in Persons. This year the international body will commemorate the day on July 30 under the theme "Trapped Behind the Scam."

"People trapped in scam compounds are victims of trafficking, forced to commit crimes through violence, threats and coercion. They deserve protection, not punishment," IOM Director General Amy Pope said in a statement. "We must work together to support survivors, stop traffickers and close the gaps these criminal networks exploit. No country can tackle this alone."

title: Spies in the sky: how worried should we be about the arrival of AI-enabled smart lamp-posts?
description:

How would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right?
fullText:
The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?

How would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? Maybe you wouldn’t mind, given how long we’ve had automatic number plate recognition and CCTV. What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right? This is what Conflow Power Group (CPG) in Warwickshire claims for its iLamps, the first of their kind in the UK.

What if lamp-posts had the potential to incorporate new AI capability – gait analysis, suspicious behaviours – that you haven’t even heard of? This is what the organisation Big Brother Watch worries about. And what if the home secretary had explicitly said she believed in a “panopticon state” – that is, a state that could watch you at all times (as Shabana Mahmood already has) – and what if she still had a job when the lamp-post eyes got their updates? Or what if the next home secretary was even keener on hyper-surveillance (hard to imagine), and the street apparatus was already in place? What about all the data this would harvest – who would own it?

It’s drizzling in Warwickshire, where I’m hoping to answer at least some of these questions in the hospital car park where some of these new “smart” lamp-posts have been installed. But if it wasn’t for me, nobody would probably be talking about them, not least because few have heard anything about them. Not many people know that the iLamp is not just solar-powered but can “double as a revenue-generating distributed AI datacentre”, according to CPG, let alone what that means. And nobody, not even me, knows how much of that potential functionality has been realised in the UK model – only what CPG has announced: that it has signed an agreement with the government of Katsina state, Nigeria, to supply it with 50,000 of these iLamps, which have additional surveillance potential for both vehicles and faces. CPG’s chairman, Edward Fitzpatrick, told the BBC World Service’s Tech Life programme that the lamp-posts could ultimately track down missing persons or fight crime, with the proviso that this would only be developed in partnership “with the relevant authority”.

CPG has been “extensively covered by worldwide media”, according to its own statement, and doesn’t take further questions, directing the media to its online material. As for the Warwickshire lamp-posts, the local authority directs all questions to the hospital, and the hospital doesn’t respond. Fair play – it’s a hospital.

A number of local residents have taken refuge from the rain in a bus shelter, most of them waiting for a partner to pick them up, and many are willing to chat. Karl, 52, who has been in a pub nearby, speaks for almost everyone when he says: “The town centre is already full of cameras, and it’s fine. You don’t mind them being there unless you’re up to no good.” No amount of loaded questions (What if you were doing something that was legal today but illegal in a year? What if the surveillance became predictive rather than reactive? What if you didn’t want anyone to know you’d been to the hospital? What if you weren’t supposed to be in a pub? Don’t you think you should at least have been asked whether you wanted it?) can separate anyone I speak to from the view that facial recognition is a tolerable part of life for a right-thinking citizen.

Tejal, 41, also waiting at the hospital bus stop, says: “I think we have to move on and accept that things change.” She’s a radiologist, and just seeing AI’s capability in her own sector makes her extremely anxious about AI as a whole. “I have anxieties for my children,” she says. That they won’t find entry-level jobs? “That, and that they’ll lose the ability to celebrate and find joy from the things we used to.” Privacy concerns do seem comparatively minor, compared with that.

Policy and technical experts are sceptical about some of the claims made for smart lamp-posts. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, says: “We see this quite often where local councils or other government agencies are … ‘swindled’ is a strong word, but they’re sold these tools as magic wands when there are limitations to what they can actually do.”

Prof Rabih Bashroush, director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Data Innovation at the University of East London, is blunt: “AI datacentres? There’s absolutely no chance this will fly: the technology doesn’t work, there’s not enough power, the economics won’t work …” Solar power to run the iLamps off-grid might work in Nigeria, but in Britain the amount generated by the lamp-posts is “negligible”, he says. You might be able to run an app that was “not mission critical, that you didn’t mind shutting down for a few days” – such as recognising whether a parking spot was occupied – but bigger claims for facial recognition are “just hype. Forget it – this has no legs.”

If he sounds impatient, it’s because he is: “It’s getting more and more difficult to get an independent opinion on things, because a lot of experts are in the industry now, and their view would have to align with their organisation,” he says. So a company might make a large claim, including a few AI buzzwords, ahead of a funding round; engineers don’t contradict them, local authorities don’t understand them and nobody else is even aware that anything has moved on since CCTV was invented.

Chaggar goes to great lengths to explain the conceptual difference between facial recognition and CCTV: “Facial recognition is not just passively recalling something, unlike CCTV, which you then check after the fact. What facial recognition does is real-time identity check: it’s much more like a fingerprint or DNA. It’s not like a passport – you can’t get another face.”

Another problem, Chaggar says, is that, “a lot of these technologies and infrastructures have capacity to add function later. Hammersmith and Fulham [in London] are updating their CCTV and it’s possible to embed facial recognition, monitor suspicious shopping behaviour, add aggression detection. So you can just turn the switch and it’s all there overnight.” A friend who lives in Fulham sent, by chance, a picture of a camera above a parking restrictions sign – it looks like a cross between Darth Vader and a beetle, and it whirrs as you go past, as if to indicate that it’s following your movements.

This throws up all the ageless privacy concerns, and it’s interesting how many people will wave away CCTV as a fact of modern life, but spontaneously raise how much they absolutely hate being listened to by their phone. Karl says: “I was talking to my mother the other day about dog nail clippers, and the advert came up on my phone that evening. I had my microphone off. I don’t even have a dog!” His friend Bob, 48, has ended up functionally off-grid, with no computer and a basic brick phone – a policymaker would probably describe him as “excluded” – simply because “some people like to be private”.

Another question about facial recognition software is: exactly how good are algorithms at detecting aggression and suspicious behaviour? “A lot of the software is pseudo-scientific,” Chaggar says. “So a company might try to sell emotion-detection, [claiming that] if people are walking through a train station, you can see if they’re angry or they’re about to be aggressive. There’s very little evidence to suggest that it’s accurate. If you’re a disabled person who moves differently, you might be flagged and have an intervention.” But the real question local authorities and any agents of the state should ask themselves, Chaggar says, is: “Are you happy to have your political enemies having these capabilities? Because you’re building an infrastructure that is here to stay.”

You can see that writ large in policing – the Home Office signed off on the use of facial recognition more than a decade ago, and the police have been “essentially using the public as guinea pigs for the past 10 years,” Chaggar says. What happens when the home secretary tells BBC 5 Live, as she did earlier this year, that “you can’t enjoy any of your liberties in any country if you’re not safe”? This sledgehammer logic, in which all liberties are secondary to the state’s rights as your protector, is chilling from a supposedly leftwing government. But the greater worry is that this doesn’t feel like the right time in politics to roll the dice on surveillance technology, basing our acceptance of it on the assumption that all future governments will be pro-social and democratic.

Wherever there’s potential to collect data, it throws up the question of who owns it: Bashroush used to work with the Internet of Things, the European Commission’s attempt to “connect the physical world to a digital environment”. “This was way back, before exiting Europe,” he remembers. “One of the challenges we saw was with a supplier [who was] basically collecting garbage from homes in the Netherlands, then optimising truck journeys and planning, based on your habits. The council that ran the programme was very happy with it, and tried to open the bidding a year later to get a more competitive price. The company said, ‘Sure, but the data is ours.’” That never got resolved: the contracts had been poorly constructed and the local authority lost the data.

If you want to see facial recognition go wrong without even any authoritarian intent or tech chicanery, you just have to look at the retail sector, where it’s already widely in use to prevent shoplifting. “We’ve seen misidentification by the police,” Chaggar says, “but in retail, when people are misidentified, it’s Kafkaesque. You’re just blacklisted from the store.”

And again, how much do people care, really? If you’re not allowed in a shop and you don’t know why; if a private company has a contract with your NHS trust, vaunting tech that isn’t operational yet and might never work, but nobody told, let alone asked, you; if the home secretary thinks it’s fine for the eyes of the state to be on you at all times – are these the building blocks of a dystopia, or do they just remind us how we used to describe dystopia, back before these surveillance capabilities existed?

The New Yorker essayist Ted Chiang wrote some time ago about the habit of projecting on to AI negatives that were actually not about tech but about economic systems, concluding: “Capitalism is the machine that will do whatever it takes to prevent us from turning it off.” Am I projecting on to AI and surveillance tech anxieties that are really about authoritarian politics?

“Well, if you haven’t got anything to hide,” says Sarah, 55, “I can’t see how it would be a problem. I’m presuming they’re actually lamps as well?”
